---
title: "What is settled, and what is current work"
subtitle: "How much weight each quantity can carry"
---

A short guide to how much weight each quantity can carry.

## Ready to use

The per-opportunity quantities are the ones to report: first differences on the
tie-presence scale, second differences for interactions, each split by creation and
maintenance margin, and averaged either at the observed waves or along
model-implied ministeps.

They are well defined, they are implemented, and their interpretation is the one
stated in Chapter 2: a probability change *per decision opportunity*, holding the
decision situation fixed.

Ego-level covariates are perturbed across the whole choice set rather than one
alternative at a time, for the reason given in the aside in Chapter 2. That happens
by itself, so the per-tie numbers you get for a sender effect are sound; they are
just a narrow summary of it. The probability-mass contrast is the fuller one, and it
is what to reach for before drawing conclusions about covariate sender effects.

## Comparability

Meta-analysing marginal effects rather than parameters is usually motivated by
some combination of five claims. They hold up differently, and two are worth
spelling out.

| claim | how it holds up |
|---|---|
| more meaningful than meta-analysing parameters | yes — a pooled coefficient averages quantities whose scales need not match |
| challenges "the same model for all networks" | yes, as a question worth asking rather than an answer already given |
| the exact same specification is less necessary | in part, and it rests on an assumption — below |
| the main advantage is a common scale | yes, though a common unit is not invariance — below |
| compare within networks, then those comparisons across networks | yes, and arguably the strongest of the five |

**On the specification.** Pooling probability-scale quantities is more forgiving
than pooling coefficients, since the numbers at least share units. But an effect
missing from one network's specification does not simply drop out: what a model
leaves unexplained is folded into everything else, so the remaining coefficients
contract and their AMEs move with them. Treating a non-estimable effect as a true
zero is an assumption about that network rather than something the scale provides —
reasonable where the effect really is negligible there, and worth stating rather
than leaving implicit.

**On the common scale.** The probability scale gives a common unit and an
interpretable quantity: the effective impact of a mechanism on decisions, in that
network's actual conditions. What it does not give is invariance. Where two
networks genuinely differ in how predictable their actors' decisions are, the same
underlying preference translates into different probability shifts — and an effect
size that comes out differently there is reporting something true. A difference in
AMEs identifies a difference in effective impact, noise included by construction;
it does not identify a difference in preferences.

## Accumulating to a whole period

Everything in Chapter 2 is per decision opportunity. A natural next question is what
a mechanism contributes over a whole period between two waves, and the
straightforward answer is to add the per-ministep effects along a simulated
sequence.

This has one clear advantage: it absorbs the rate parameter. Two networks whose
actors decide at very different frequencies can have the same per-opportunity effect
but very different period-level pressure, and only the accumulated version reflects
that — which makes it the natural candidate when opportunity rates differ across the
networks being compared.

The scale needs care, though. An additive sum of probability changes is a count —
extra ties created plus dissolutions avoided over the period — not a probability. It
is not bounded, and it should not be set against a between-wave difference in tie
proportions: a dyad that creates a tie and later drops it contributes twice to the
count while changing prevalence not at all. So read ratios across specifications,
which sit on a common scale, rather than levels on their own.

Getting from that count to a genuinely bounded, prevalence-scale period quantity is
current work. The construction follows the tie's own two-state history rather than
summing increments; it is derived but not implemented, so it is not available in the
software yet.

## The rate parameter

Rate effects sit outside everything above, and that is a scope choice rather than an
oversight: any count-level quantity mixes how *often* actors decide with what they
choose given the chance, and separating the two needs its own treatment. The rate
parameter is best read as governing how quickly a dyad's situation can change, not
where it ends up.

## Further reading

The SAOM itself is set out in @Snijders01 and, at book length, in @AMAND. For
marginal effects generally, @LongMustillo2021 is the closest thing to a standard
reference, and @Glasgow2022 covers the discrete-choice side. On the ERGM side,
@Duxbury2023 sets out the scaling problem and @Duxbury2026 develops effect sizes
for structural terms; @IndlekoferBrandes2013 is the nearest existing SAOM tool.
